title: General Survey and Basic Observation

sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Two things make the general survey different from the rest of the exam: it covers the whole person rather than one part, and it never really stops. The moment you see someone, you already have data, and you keep collecting it while you talk and examine. A useful test: if a finding required you to pick a body region first, it is not the general survey. If you would have noticed it standing in the doorway, it is.

### Question 2

The four categories map onto four different questions: how does the person look, how are they built, how do they move, and how do they act. Grouping observations this way keeps you from noticing only the dramatic thing and missing the rest. The other answer choices are all real assessment lists, which is exactly the trap; the way to sort them out is to ask whether the list requires equipment, a stethoscope, or a set of test questions, because the general survey requires none of those.

### Question 3

Inspection sounds passive, but clinically it means looking on purpose, with a plan, rather than glancing. It is also not limited to the eyes; hearing someone's speech break into short bursts, or smelling a fruity odor on the breath, is inspection data too. The reason it comes first is practical: the other three techniques all require you to already know where on the body to aim, and inspection is what tells you where.

### Question 4

The survey answers a scheduling question, not a diagnostic one: how much time do I have, and what do I do first. That is why it belongs at the very start. Notice what it cannot do. It cannot give you a number, so it never replaces taking vital signs, and it cannot name a disease. And it is never used to judge whether the patient's reported symptoms are real; observation and self-report are two different kinds of data, not a check on each other.

### Question 5

The dividing line is not equipment and it is not who wrote it down; it is whether a second person standing in the room could confirm it. Nobody else can feel the patient's weakness, so that stays subjective no matter how carefully it is charted. Anyone watching could confirm a wide-based, unsteady gait, so it is objective even though no device was used. Watch the direction of the error in the wrong answers: one demands a machine, the other assumes the nurse's authority is what makes data objective.

### Question 6

Hemoglobin changes color depending on whether it is carrying oxygen: bright red when loaded, dark bluish-red when unloaded. Cyanosis appears where skin is thin enough to show that darker blood, which is why lips and nail beds are the places to look. The clinically important catch is that cyanosis depends on how much unloaded hemoglobin is present, not what fraction is unloaded. Someone with very little hemoglobin to begin with can be seriously short on oxygen and still not look blue, so never treat absent cyanosis as reassurance.

### Question 7

Anchor it to the plane you are looking from. Viewed from the side, a normal spine already curves gently outward at the chest and inward at the low back; kyphosis and lordosis are those two normal curves taken too far. Viewed from behind, a normal spine should look straight, so any sideways bend there is scoliosis. So the first question is always which direction you are looking, and only then which segment is involved.

### Question 8

Bracing the arms on something fixed gives neck and chest muscles a stable anchor to pull against, which lets them help expand the rib cage. That is why people instinctively prop their hands on their knees after sprinting, and it is why the position is a red flag when someone adopts it sitting still. Phrase length is the second clue and costs nothing to check: count the words a patient gets out per breath. Full sentences suggest reserve, three or four words at a time suggests very little.

### Question 9

The logic word changes as you move down the chart, and that is the whole trick. Normal and elevated use AND, so both numbers must qualify. Stage 1 and stage 2 use OR, so a single out-of-range number is enough. Practically, that means you classify by whichever number is worse. Here the diastolic of 86 already rules out elevated on its own, and 134 systolic lands in the 130 to 139 band, so both routes lead to stage 1. Classification also assumes proper technique and a confirming reading, which the stem supplies.

### Question 10

A good test before charting: could a colleague who never met this patient check your note against the patient tomorrow and agree or disagree with it? Descriptions pass that test; labels do not. "Difficult" cannot be verified or tracked, and it quietly shapes how the next clinician treats the person before they walk in. "Declined to answer questions about medications and turned toward the wall" can be verified, and it can change, which is exactly what makes documentation clinically useful rather than merely opinionated.

### Question 11

Two of the most useful general survey observations cost nothing: whether someone looks their stated age, and whether their clothes still fit them. Both are indirect ways of reading body composition over time, which no single visit measurement can show you. The disciplined move is to stop at the level the observation supports. You have evidence that this body has changed, and that is enough to justify asking about weight, appetite, and intake. It is not enough to name a cause, and the list of possible causes is long.

### Question 12

Fever is a response the body has to generate, and that capacity weakens with age, so its absence carries much less reassurance in an 82-year-old than in a 25-year-old. This is also why baseline matters more than the printed normal range: a jump from someone's usual 97.0 to 99.0 can be meaningful even though both numbers look unremarkable on their own. The signal to trust here is the change the family reports. Sudden confusion is an acute finding demanding a cause, not a feature of getting older.
